extracted.intended_audience: researchers in computational humor and NLP; dataset builders interested in humor annotation
extracted.subtask_description: Designing and releasing a crowd-annotated Spanish corpus of tweets for computational humor tasks (recognition, generation, scoring), with annotations for humor value and funniness and measured inter-annotator agreement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Humor annotation (humor value)
rubrics_metrics.description: Tweets are crowd-annotated by their humor value.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use human (crowd) judgments to label whether a tweet is humorous or not; the dataset provides such binary/qualitative humor-value annotations across items.

rubrics_metrics.name: Funniness score
rubrics_metrics.description: Tweets are annotated by a funniness score in addition to humor value.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Collect per-item graded ratings of how funny a tweet is (a funniness score) from annotators to capture intensity of humor, not just binary presence/absence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Number of annotations per item (~4)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Obtain multiple independent annotations for each tweet (the authors used approximately four annotations per item) to enable aggregation and reliability estimation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Annotator pool size and diversity
rubrics_metrics.description: Tagged by 1,300 people over the Internet.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use a relatively large and diverse crowd of annotators (the corpus used ~1,300 distinct annotators) to capture varied perceptions and reduce individual bias.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balanced sourcing between humorous and non-humorous accounts
rubrics_metrics.description: It is equally divided between tweets coming from humorous and non-humorous accounts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When constructing the corpus, ensure class/source balance (the dataset was intentionally split equally between tweets from 'humorous' accounts and 'non-humorous' accounts) to avoid source bias.

rubrics_metrics.name: Corpus size and scope
rubrics_metrics.description: A corpus of 27,000 tweets written in Spanish.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide sizable data (27,000 items) in the target language (Spanish) and genre (tweets) to support model training and evaluation for humor tasks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Measure inter-annotator agreement (Krippendorff's alpha)
rubrics_metrics.description: Inter-annotator agreement Krippendorff's alpha value is 0.5710.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report and use standard agreement statistics (the paper reports Krippendorff's alpha = 0.5710) to quantify annotator consistency and to inform downstream use of annotations given subjectivity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intended task applicability
rubrics_metrics.description: Dataset can serve as a basis for humor detection and as a first step to tackle subjectivity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design datasets with explicit intended uses (humor recognition, generation, scoring) and with annotation schemes that enable studying subjectivity in humor judgments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Crowdsourcing annotation methodology
rubrics_metrics.description: Crowd-annotated by their humor value and funniness score, tagged by 1,300 people over the Internet.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopt an online crowdsourcing approach for collecting annotations; document the annotation scheme (what was asked), the number of annotators per item, and the annotator recruitment method to allow reproducibility and interpretation.
